name: The Bail Project: policy, public education and research (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: people kept out of pretrial detention by the US state campaigns (Texas, Florida, Oklahoma and others).
summary: The Bail Project's policy, public-education and research work (about $5 million a year with overhead, fiscal 2023-2025) campaigns in the states where it bails people out, and its wins of those years are counted as a past average: shares of the defeat of Texas's 2023 bail-denial amendment and personal-bond bill (held off two years, until Proposition 3 and SB 9 passed in 2025, plus a twentieth of Proposition 3's effect through the protections it carries), of the defeat of two further denial amendments in 2025 (sized on their sponsor's own figure), and of blocking a year's bills against charitable bail in Florida and Oklahoma, each valued as the detention, sentences, lost earnings, jail costs and deaths avoided, with the bail model's shared figures, the Texas measures sized on Harris County's flow of eligible defendants and its prosecutors' first months of no-bail hearings; the campaigns it lost count nothing. The result is about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, low because the wins are defensive and short-lived, the charity's share of the coalitions is small and the next dollar counts at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the average, with years of spending in reserve. Every branch is discounted for missing data, and the result is mostly uncertainty: how much detention the defeated measures would have added and how much of their defeat is the campaign's.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

source.title: Houston Chronicle on the Patrick Scott bail hearing, January 2026

source.note: Four requests in the two months after Proposition 3 took effect (19 November 2025), against about 200 eligible defendants released on bond a month in 2025 (KWBU); only offences after that date qualify, so use may grow.

rows.explainer: A few percent of eligible defendants in Harris County's first months, with room to grow as eligible cases accumulate: 5% (1% to 20%).

rows.label: Texas: people a year held without bail under Proposition 3 statewide
rows.explainer: Harris's eligible flow, scaled to the state by its share of the jail population, times the share prosecutors get held: about 900 people a year.

rows.label: Texas: person-years of detention a year Proposition 3 adds statewide
rows.explainer: People held times the extra days each is held.

rows.label: Texas: extra days held per person denied bail
rows.explainer: For defendants charged with the listed offences the average stay in Harris County's jail is 280 days (KWBU and Fox 26 Houston, from the county's analysis); people held without bail stay about that long, and some would have paid bail weeks or months in, so the extra time is less: 200 days (120 to 280), our judgment.

rows.label: Texas 2023: denial of bail under the defeated SJR 44, against Proposition 3's
rows.explainer: SJR 44 as passed by the Senate covered any violent offence, the House committee's version five offences mostly with a deadly weapon; Proposition 3 sits between. Similar in scope: 1 (0.6 to 1.3), our judgment.

rows.label: Texas 2023: share of listed-offence defendants released on personal bonds
rows.explainer: SB 1318 (and SB 9, its return in 2025) bars personal bonds, release without money, for the listed offences. The reference class is Harris County's felony bonds: most felony defendants released there post cash or surety bail, and personal bonds go mostly to lower-level charges, so a minority of the violent felonies listed. Our judgment: 25% (10% to 50%).

rows.label: Texas 2023: share of them who couldn't post the cash bail set instead
rows.explainer: Of people who would get a personal bond, the share who couldn't post the cash or surety bail set instead. The reference class is the people charitable bail serves: those held on bail they can't pay, against the 55% of defendants Dobbie et al. find out within three days, most by paying. Our judgment: 30% (10% to 50%), held until their case closes. This term doesn't scale with prosecutors' denial motions.

rows.label: Texas 2023: people a year SB 1318 would have held on cash bail they couldn't pay
rows.explainer: The statewide eligible flow on personal bonds who couldn't pay.

rows.label: Texas 2023: people a year who would have been held
rows.explainer: Denial under SJR 44 plus the cash-bail holds under SB 1318.

rows.label: Texas 2023: person-years of detention a year the defeated measures would have added
rows.explainer: People held times the extra days each is held.

rows.label: Texas 2023: years the defeat held the expansion off
rows.explainer: SB 1318 would have taken effect on 1 September 2023 and its content returned in SB 9 from 1 September 2025; SJR 44 would have gone to the November 2023 ballot and Proposition 3, approved on 4 November 2025, applies to offences from 19 November 2025 by the Texas District and County Attorneys Association's reading (1 January 2026 in CBS News Texas's report); either way. About two years, as a won reform later repealed counts its years in force.

source.title: CBS News Texas, Texans approve Proposition 3, expanding judges' power to deny bail in violent, sexual felony cases

rows.label: Texas 2023: wait from the defeat until the measures would have taken effect
rows.explainer: Both measures died on the House floor on 23 May 2023, the deadline for Senate bills; they would have applied from September to late November 2023: 0.4 years (0.25 to 0.5).

source.title: Texas Legislature Online, history of SJR 44 (88th Legislature)

rows.label: Texas 2023: share of Proposition 3's added detention avoided by the protections in the 2025 text
rows.explainer: The charity 'led a coalition of state and national partners' on SJR 5 (2025 report) and calls it a mixed win, naming the right to counsel at bail hearings; most of its protections (a hearing, written findings, the clear-and-convincing standard) were already in the House's 2023 SJR 44. Our judgment: 5% (0 to 20%) of Proposition 3's added detention, applied after the two years.

rows.label: Texas 2023: years counted, discounted
rows.formula: (pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, tx_delay_years) + tx_mitigation_share * prop3_detyears_per_year / tx_detyears_per_year * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, $win_years_counted) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - tx_delay_years)) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - tx_years_until_effect)
rows.explainer: The two years held off, plus the protections' share of Proposition 3's detention over the site's years counted for a won reform after them, all after the wait.

rows.label: Texas 2023: share of the defeat due to the opposition campaign
rows.explainer: SJR 44 and SB 1318 passed the Senate (30-1 and 31-0) and were postponed on the House floor on the deadline day: partly a calendar death, which the opposition's floor work helped bring about. A share of an outcome already in, not a chance still to be drawn: 30% (10% to 60%), our judgment.

rows.label: Texas: the charity's share of the coalition's resources
rows.explainer: The named coalition members spent $21.5 million in their latest years (ACLU Foundation of Texas $4.1M, Texas Civil Rights Project $7.4M, Texas Appleseed $8.9M, Texas Fair Defense Project $1.1M; ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, 2023 Forms 990), perhaps a tenth of it on bail and pretrial work, beside public defenders and national groups; the charity's own Texas share of its $1.2 million policy budget and of its research is about $0.5 million. Its share: 15% (5% to 30%).

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): governments' budgets and enforcement, companies' compliance, the use others make of research. The charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work. Fixed.

rows.label: Texas: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Texas 2023: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The shared validity of the release effects.

rows.label: Texas 2023: share of the win delivered
rows.explainer: A defeated amendment and bill change nothing that needs enforcing; the 2025 protections' application is in their share.

rows.label: Texas 2023: missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: the detention the measures would have added is judged, so the site's discount for missing data applies.

rows.label: Texas 2023: all adjustments
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

source.title: Texas Tribune, Proposal to automatically deny bail to some previously accused of felonies falls in Texas House, 26 May 2025
source.quote: an effective class of people that amounts to 0.0084% of our population
source.note: The sponsor, Rep. Mitch Little; SJR 87 would have denied bail automatically to people accused of nine listed felonies with a prior felony conviction or already out on bond.

rows.explainer: The sponsor's own size, unverified, so half to twice it.

rows.label: Texas 2025: share of listed-offence defendants SJR 1 would have denied bail as non-citizens without legal status
rows.explainer: SJR 1 would have denied bail to people in the country illegally charged with some felonies. The reference class is the unauthorised share of Texas's population, about 5 to 7% of Texas's population (Pew Research Center's 1.6 million for 2022, the Department of Homeland Security's 2.06 million; about 8% of its workforce); it is taken lower for defendants charged with the listed violent felonies, whose charge rates studies of Texas arrest data find no higher, and often lower, than citizens'. Our judgment: 5% (2% to 10%) of the listed-offence defendants.

rows.label: Texas 2025: people a year the defeated SJR 87 and SJR 1 would have held
rows.explainer: SJR 87's class and SJR 1's non-citizens, less those prosecutors already get held under Proposition 3 (the offences overlap).

rows.label: Texas 2025: person-years of detention a year the defeated measures would have added
rows.explainer: People held times the extra days each is held.

rows.label: Texas 2025: years until a similar measure passes
rows.explainer: The legislature meets next in 2027; a measure passed then would apply from late 2027: 2 years (1.5 to 4).

rows.label: Texas 2025: wait from the defeat until the measures would have taken effect
rows.explainer: Defeated in May-June 2025; they would have gone to the November 2025 ballot: half a year.

rows.label: Texas 2025: years counted, discounted
rows.explainer: The years held off, after the wait.

rows.label: Texas 2025: share of the defeat due to the opposition campaign
rows.explainer: SJR 87 and SJR 1 died in the House in 2025, where the Senate's bail measures have twice failed at the floor stage; the opposition's floor work is one reason among the calendar and the House's own priorities. A share of an outcome already in: 30% (10%, if they would have died anyway, to 60%, if the campaign turned the votes), as for the 2023 measures.

rows.label: Texas 2025: the charity's share of the coalition's resources
rows.explainer: The same coalition as in 2023, but the charity's annual report claims SJR 5, not these defeats, so a lower share: 8% (2% to 20%).

rows.label: Texas 2025: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Texas 2025: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The shared validity of the release effects.

rows.label: Texas 2025: share of the win delivered
rows.explainer: Defeated measures need no enforcement.

rows.label: Texas 2025: missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin, as the 2023 branch.

rows.label: Texas 2025: all adjustments
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Texas 2023: homes kept, WELLBYs a year
rows.explainer: Not counted for people held for months under denial of bail: a home lost then is in the shared life-satisfaction loss of the months inside and in the earnings of release.

rows.label: Texas 2025: homes kept, WELLBYs a year
rows.explainer: Not counted for people held for months under denial of bail: a home lost then is in the shared life-satisfaction loss of the months inside and in the earnings of release.

rows.label: The charity's bailouts a year (fiscal 2025)
rows.explainer: The shared estimate, as in the bail model: about {{row:cb_tbp_bailouts}}.

rows.label: Share of the charity's bailouts at its Florida and Oklahoma sites
rows.explainer: Five of its 14 bail sites (Jacksonville, Orlando, Pensacola, Oklahoma City, Tulsa; 2025 report): 36% (25% to 45%).

rows.label: Other charitable bail funds' bailouts there, as a share of the charity's
rows.explainer: Local community bail funds in the two states are small beside the charity's sites: 20% (0 to 60%), our judgment.

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: charitable bailouts a year the bills threatened
rows.explainer: About 1,400.

rows.label: Share of those bailouts lost had the restrictions passed
rows.explainer: Georgia's SB 63 (2024) stopped the charity's bailouts there until a preliminary injunction in a suit brought by others; elsewhere funds would move their money to other states, where it frees others, after a lag. Our judgment: half lost while the restriction stood (20% to 90%).

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: people a year kept out of detention
rows.explainer: Bailouts kept, times the shared share of the days clients would really have served.

rows.label: Days of detention avoided per bailout
rows.explainer: The charity's own days over the year's bailouts, as in the bail model: about 25.

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: person-years of detention avoided a year
rows.explainer: People times days held.

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: years until the next attempt
rows.explainer: The bail bond industry brings the bills back each session: Florida's HB 1017 and SB 600 (2026, died 13 March 2026) and Oklahoma's SB 1878 and SB 1705 (introduced January 2026). A block holds until the next session's bill, whose outcome is its own win: 1 year (1 to 3).

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: years counted, discounted
rows.explainer: The years the block holds; it takes effect at once.

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: homes kept, WELLBYs a year
rows.explainer: As in the bail model: the shared share of clients who would lose a home in weeks of detention, its loss and the time to rehouse.

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: share of the bills' defeat due to the opposition
rows.explainer: The charity says it 'decisively blocked' the industry's 2025 bills; we found no public record naming them (the 2026 bills are on record), so the claim rests on its report. A share of an outcome already in: 30% (10% to 60%), our judgment.

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: the charity's share of the opposition's resources
rows.explainer: The bills targeted charitable bail and the charity is by far the largest fund in both states; local funds, defenders and civil-liberties groups joined: 40% (20% to 70%).

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The shared validity of the release effects.

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: share of the value kept after missed court dates
rows.explainer: As in the bail model: about 0.98.

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: leverage and funging of the bail kept
rows.explainer: As in the bail model: 0.95.

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: what the bills would have done is judged.

rows.label: Florida and Oklahoma: all adjustments
rows.formula: cb_counterfactual_adj * cb_attribution_share * cb_evidence_adj * cb_implementation_adj * cb_leverage_funging_adj * cb_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.formula: ((tx_detyears_per_year + tx_people_per_year * sentence_years_per_release) * ls_gain_per_person_year + tx_housing_wellbys) * tx_discounted_years * tx_total_adj / campaign_years
rows.explainer: Detention and sentence years avoided times the shared life-satisfaction loss, plus homes kept, over the years counted, adjusted, per year of campaigns.

rows.label: Texas 2023: income, public money and deaths a year of campaigning, in units of value, adjusted
rows.formula: (tx_people_per_year * ln_gain_per_release * $uov_per_ln_consumption + (tx_detyears_per_year + tx_people_per_year * sentence_years_per_release) * (365 * @incarceration.jail_cost_per_day * public_uov_per_dollar + deaths_per_long_detention_year * value_per_death)) * tx_discounted_years * tx_total_adj / campaign_years
rows.explainer: Released people's earnings, the jail costs saved on detention and sentence days (the shared marginal cost of a day) and the deaths detention causes, over the years counted, adjusted, per year of campaigns.

rows.label: Side effect: backlash, as a share of the value
rows.explainer: Charitable bail's visibility helps the bail bond industry's campaigns against it (Georgia 2024, the bills of 2025 and 2026); the campaigns the charity lost (Georgia's SB 63 in 2024, Texas's SB 9 and Proposition 3 in 2025) are already at zero value here. -3% (-15% to 0), our judgment.

rows.label: Side effect: children and partners spared a parent's detention, as a share of the Florida and Oklahoma branch's value
rows.explainer: The shared figure for weeks of detention, as in the bail model: {{row:ue_family}} (0 to 30%).

rows.label: Side effect: children and partners spared a parent's months of detention, as a share of the Texas branches' value
rows.explainer: Months of pretrial detention separate families as a prison term does: the shared share of a prison-year's value that falls on partners and children (facts/incarceration.json, Wakefield and Wildeman 2013), {{row:ue_family_tx}}, from 0 to 40%.

rows.label: Side effect: crime by people bailed out in Florida and Oklahoma, as a share of that branch's value
rows.explainer: The shared figure, as in the bail model: {{row:ue_crime_cb}} (-20% to +5%).

rows.label: Side effect: crime by people charged with violent felonies who stay out, as a share of the Texas branches' value
rows.explainer: The Texas measures cover people charged with violent and sexual felonies, held for months; their risk while out is higher than the average client's and the time out longer. Prison Policy Initiative's ue_dec_crime, -10% (-30% to 0), for people kept out of prison is the reference class.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Prison Policy Initiative (rows ue_dec_family and ue_dec_crime)
